label: Manifolds By Gluing
notes: Open with the chapter's core stance: a manifold can be specified by local models plus gluing instructions. The deck follows printed pages 3 through 42 and the matching notebook. The lecture moves from polygon identification pictures, to hyperbolic surfaces in the disk, to Euler-characteristic bookkeeping, and finishes with first three-manifold examples.

label: Atlas-By-Identification
notes: Before drawing anything, fix the mental model. A manifold near a point looks Euclidean. Globally it is assembled by gluing local pieces along instructions. Stress that the gluing data is the manifold; the embedding is optional. The notebook treats the square-to-torus and octagon-to-genus-two pairings as the first laboratory.

label: Square To Torus
notes: Walk through the square with opposite sides identified. Match the arrows on top and bottom, and on the two vertical sides. All four corners collapse to a single point. The result is a torus with Euler characteristic zero and genus one. The slide deliberately leaves the abstract surface unembedded; the arrows are the manifold.

label: Octagon Genus Two
notes: Repeat the bookkeeping for the side word a b a-inverse b-inverse c d c-inverse d-inverse. Eight sides, four arrow types, all eight vertices identified to one. The Euler-characteristic formula gives 1 minus 4 plus 1 equals minus two, so the surface has genus two. This is the first hint that polygon words classify orientable surfaces.

label: Hyperbolic Disk
notes: Switch from polygon pictures to the Poincare disk. Hyperbolic lines are Euclidean arcs orthogonal to the boundary circle, and isometries are Mobius maps preserving the disk. A genus-two hyperbolic surface is a disk octagon with hyperbolic side identifications. The orthogonality is checkable numerically in the notebook.

label: Euler Ledger
notes: Pause on Euler characteristic. It is invariant under cell subdivision, additive on connected sums up to a correction, and equal to the sum of vector-field indices on the surface. The slide presents these three facts as one ledger: every operation either preserves chi or changes it predictably. That is what makes it a classification tool.

label: Index Catalog
notes: Introduce vector-field indices as the dynamical witness for Euler characteristic. A sphere admits no nonvanishing vector field; a torus does. The slide draws representative singularities (source, sink, saddle) with their index values plus or minus one, and reminds students that the sum equals chi for any tangent vector field with isolated zeros.

label: Cube To Three-Torus
notes: Move the gluing imagination to three dimensions. A cube with opposite faces identified produces the three-torus. Emphasize that the local model is the open three-ball; the gluing is on the boundary. The slide also names the new bookkeeping question: which edges and vertices identify, and what does the resulting universe look like?

label: Three-Manifold Zoo
notes: Show the four representative three-manifolds from the chapter: the three-torus, real projective three-space from a ball with antipodal boundary points, lens spaces from solid-torus slope gluings, and the dodecahedral example. The point is variety, not a classification statement. Each one is a gluing recipe.

label: Applied Lab
notes: Walk through the applied lab. For a standard orientable polygon word with four-g sides, all vertices identify and Euler characteristic equals two minus two-g. Apply the formula to a hexagon with a b c a-inverse b-inverse c-inverse to get genus one. The lab gives students a fast checkable test before tackling the classification theorem.

label: Recap
notes: Close with the chapter takeaways. A manifold is local-model plus gluing data. The torus is the first trustworthy laboratory. Hyperbolic surfaces appear early because the disk model makes them computable. Euler characteristic, connected sum, and vector-field index turn classification into a ledger. Three-manifold examples ask for the same skill in one higher dimension.
